chapter_title: Managing Projects, Users, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
chapter_summary:
Effective management of projects, users, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is fundamental for any multi-tenant OpenShift environment. As an RHCA, you'll be responsible for ensuring that teams and applications have the necessary access without compromising the security or stability of the cluster. OpenShift leverages Kubernetes' concept of namespaces, extending it with **Projects**. A project in OpenShift is essentially a Kubernetes namespace with additional annotations and security contexts, providing a logical grouping for application resources (pods, services, routes, builds, etc.) and serving as a boundary for access control and resource quotas. Projects facilitate multi-tenancy by isolating teams and their applications from each other, preventing accidental or malicious interference.

Creating a new project is straightforward. As a cluster administrator, you can use the `oc new-project` command:
```bash
oc new-project my-dev-project --display-name="My Development Project" --description="Project for the development team"
```
This command not only creates the namespace but also automatically assigns the user who created it as the `admin` role within that project, simplifying initial setup. You can then switch to this project using `oc project my-dev-project`. For managing existing projects, commands like `oc get projects`, `oc describe project <project-name>`, and `oc delete project <project-name>` are essential. Deleting a project is a powerful operation that removes all resources within it, so exercise extreme caution.

The cornerstone of secure multi-tenancy in OpenShift is **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)**. RBAC allows you to define who (users, groups, service accounts) can perform what actions (verbs like `get`, `list`, `create`, `delete`) on which resources (pods, services, deployments) within a specific scope (cluster-wide or within a project/namespace). OpenShift builds upon Kubernetes RBAC, providing a rich set of predefined roles and making it easier to manage access. The key RBAC components are:
*   **Roles / ClusterRoles:** A `Role` defines permissions within a specific namespace/project, while a `ClusterRole` defines permissions across the entire cluster.
*   **RoleBindings / ClusterRoleBindings:** A `RoleBinding` grants the permissions defined in a `Role` (or `ClusterRole`) to a user, group, or service account within a specific namespace/project. A `ClusterRoleBinding` grants the permissions defined in a `ClusterRole` to a user, group, or service account across the entire cluster.

OpenShift provides several default `ClusterRoles` that are commonly used, such as `admin`, `edit`, `view`, and `cluster-admin`. The `admin` role grants full control over a project, `edit` allows read/write access to most resources (but not role management), and `view` provides read-only access. `cluster-admin` grants super-user access to the entire cluster.

To grant a user `jane.doe` the `edit` role within `my-dev-project`, you would use:
```bash
oc policy add-role-to-user edit jane.doe -n my-dev-project
```
To remove the role:
```bash
oc policy remove-role-from-user edit jane.doe -n my-dev-project
```
For groups, simply replace `user` with `group`:
```bash
oc policy add-role-to-group admin dev-team -n my-dev-project
```
**Service Accounts** are another critical aspect of RBAC. These are identities used by processes running in pods to interact with the Kubernetes API. By default, every pod gets a service account, and you can assign specific roles to these service accounts to control what your applications can do within the cluster. For instance, if an application needs to list pods in its own namespace, you would create a `Role` with `get`, `list` permissions on `pods` and bind it to the application's service account.

```yaml
# my-app-sa-role.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: my-dev-project
rules:
- apiGroups: [""] # "" indicates the core API group
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "watch", "list"]
---
# my-app-sa-rolebinding.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: pod-reader-binding
  namespace: my-dev-project
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: my-app-serviceaccount # Name of the service account
  namespace: my-dev-project
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```
Apply these with `oc apply -f my-app-sa-role.yaml -n my-dev-project`. Then, ensure your Deployment's pod specification uses `serviceAccountName: my-app-serviceaccount`.

A common mistake is granting overly broad permissions, especially `cluster-admin` or `admin` roles, when more specific roles would suffice. Always adhere to the **principle of least privilege**. Grant only the permissions necessary for a user or service account to perform its function. Another pitfall is not understanding the difference between `Role` and `ClusterRole` or `RoleBinding` and `ClusterRoleBinding`. Using a `ClusterRoleBinding` when a `RoleBinding` is appropriate can inadvertently grant cluster-wide permissions, creating a significant security risk. Safety-wise, regularly audit your `RoleBindings` and `ClusterRoleBindings` to ensure no unauthorized access has been granted. Use external identity providers like LDAP or OpenID Connect for user authentication instead of managing HTPasswd users, as this centralizes user management and leverages existing enterprise security policies. Also, be cautious when granting `self-provisioner` role to users, as it allows them to create new projects, which might need to be restricted in some environments.

screens.title: Managing Projects, Users, and RBAC
screens.subtitle: How OpenShift projects and RBAC keep multi-tenant clusters secure and manageable

narration.text: In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of OpenShift projects and Role-Based Access Control, and why they matter for secure multi-tenant clusters. A project in OpenShift is a namespace with additional annotations and security contexts; it groups pods, services, routes and other application resources and provides a boundary for resource quotas and access. You will learn concrete commands to create and remove projects, how the platform assigns an initial admin, and the safety implications of deleting a project. We will also unpack RBAC: the differences between Roles and ClusterRoles, how RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings grant permissions, and why service accounts need carefully scoped roles. Throughout, you will see short command examples and a hands-on activity that walks through creating a project, assigning a user the edit role, and giving an application a least-privilege service account. By the end, you’ll know how to reason about permissions, avoid common mistakes like over-privileging, and design safer access patterns for teams and applications.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Projects are namespace-backed boundaries and RBAC controls who can do what. Combine them thoughtfully to enable team autonomy while protecting the cluster.

Understand projects as isolation boundaries and use RBAC to grant precise permissions for users and service accounts.

In this module we focus on commands you will run as an administrator and the policies you will design. Pay attention to the difference between namespace-scoped Roles and cluster-scoped ClusterRoles, and the safety considerations when binding roles.

In this lesson

  • RBAC primitives: Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings, and service accounts.
Coming up

RBAC

Logical grouping, quotas, and boundary for RoleBindings.

Proper project and RBAC management prevents privilege escalation, reduces blast radius, and enables teams to work independently without compromising cluster stability.

narration.text: These objectives map directly to practical tasks you will perform as an OpenShift administrator. First, you will understand how projects act as namespace extensions and why that supports multi-tenancy: this helps you design boundaries so teams cannot accidentally interfere with each other. Second, you will be able to create, inspect, and delete projects via the oc CLI and the web console, and you will know the safety checks to run before removing a project. Third, you will learn RBAC principles and how Kubernetes roles and bindings operate in scope; this knowledge prevents accidental cluster-wide privilege grants. Fourth, you will administer users, groups, and service accounts, assigning least-privilege roles and verifying access. Each objective pairs a concrete command or manifest with the rationale for its use, so you learn both how and why. The lab activity at the end ties these objectives together by having you create a project, add a user or group with the edit role, and configure a service account with a custom RoleBinding. screens.title: What is an OpenShift Project?
screens.subtitle: Projects as namespace extensions for multi-tenancy and isolation

narration.text: A project in OpenShift is a Kubernetes namespace extended with OpenShift-specific annotations and security contexts. This extension means a project is the unit you use to group application resources — pods, services, routes, builds — and to apply quotas and access controls. The important operational claim is this: treat projects as the primary tenancy boundary. For example, a team’s development and staging environments can live in separate projects so their resources and role bindings do not overlap. A concrete example: creating my-dev-project provides a namespace with project metadata and assigns the creating user the admin role for that project. A common misconception is thinking a project automatically enforces strict network isolation; a project isolates resource names, quotas, and role binding scope, but network policies must be configured separately if you need pod-level network isolation. Key administrative consequences follow: set meaningful display names and descriptions to help audit and governance; use projects with quotas to limit resource usage; and avoid using a single project for unrelated teams. To check understanding, ask yourself: what boundaries do I need — ownership, quota limits, and role scope — and does a separate project solve each requirement? If yes, create a project; if not, consider resource policies within the same project.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A project = Kubernetes namespace + OpenShift annotations and security contexts providing logical isolation and quota boundaries.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is an OpenShift Project?
Project definition
A logical grouping backed by a Kubernetes namespace, extended with OpenShift metadata and security context to support multi-tenancy.
Key properties:
  • Groups resources and metadata for a team or application lifecycle.
  • Acts as a boundary for RoleBindings and resource quotas.
  • Does not implicitly provide network isolation; use NetworkPolicy if required.
Analogy
Think of a project like a project folder on a shared server: items inside are grouped and permissions are applied at the folder level, but internal organization still needs policies.
Concrete example
oc new-project my-dev-project --display-name="My Development Project" --description="Project for the development team"
This command creates the namespace and assigns the creating user the admin role in that project.
Checks and common mistakes
  • Before deleting a project, list resources and backups — deletion removes all contained resources.
  • Avoid lumping unrelated teams into one project; it increases blast radius and complicates quotas.
  • Remember: project != network isolation. Add NetworkPolicies if needed.
Key Takeaway

Use projects as ownership and quota boundaries; pair them with network or image policies if you need tighter isolation.

screens.title: Create, Inspect, and Delete Projects
screens.subtitle: Common oc commands and safe practices for project lifecycle

narration.text: Knowing the commands and their effects is essential when you manage projects. The typical workflow begins with oc new-project to create a namespace and informative metadata. That command also assigns the creating user admin privilege in the new project, which simplifies initial setup. After creation, oc get projects and oc describe project let you inspect status, annotations, and applied quotas. Deleting a project via oc delete project is destructive: it removes all resources in the namespace. A concrete step you should always take before deletion is to list resources and export any required manifests or backups. For example, oc get all -n my-dev-project and oc get pvc -n my-dev-project help identify persistent volumes or services needing preservation. A common misconception is that deleting the project will always be fast; depending on finalizers and resources, deletion can hang — inspect finalizers and check the project status. In practical terms, use oc project to switch context when running many commands, and confirm you are in the right project to avoid accidental operations. This walkthrough will show command examples you will run in the lab and verification steps to ensure safety.

keyIdea.title: Command checklist
keyIdea.text: Use oc new-project, oc get/describe, oc project to switch context, and oc delete with careful verification and backups.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Create, Inspect, and Delete Projects
Typical commands
oc new-project my-dev-project --display-name="My Development Project" --description="Project for the development team"
oc project my-dev-project
oc get projects
oc describe project my-dev-project
oc delete project my-dev-project
Run oc project to switch your current namespace and reduce risk of operating in the wrong project.
Safety checklist before deletion
  • List resources: oc get all -n <project>, oc get pvc -n <project>.
  • Export manifests for important objects and backups for persistent data.
  • Check for finalizers and long-running build or operator tasks that may block deletion.
Common pitfalls
  • Assuming deletion is instant; verify project status and look for blocked finalizers.
  • Failing to confirm context — an oc delete in the wrong project can be catastrophic.
Pro tip

Use descriptive display names and descriptions when creating projects to ease future audits and ownership tracking.

screens.title: RBAC Fundamentals in OpenShift
screens.subtitle: Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, and ClusterRoleBindings explained

narration.text: Role-Based Access Control is the mechanism that lets you define who can perform which actions on which resources, and at what scope. In OpenShift RBAC, the core objects are Role and ClusterRole, which declare permissions as verbs like get, list, create, or delete on resource types such as pods or services. Roles are namespace-scoped while ClusterRoles apply cluster-wide. To grant a role’s permissions to an identity you use RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding. RoleBinding ties a role to a user, group, or service account within a namespace; ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole across the entire cluster. A practical example: using oc policy add-role-to-user edit jane. doe -n my-dev-project is a convenience that creates a RoleBinding so the user has edit permissions in that project. A common misconception is assuming ClusterRoleBindings are safe for convenience — they are not. Creating a ClusterRoleBinding can inadvertently grant wide access across the cluster. When deciding which to use, prefer a RoleBinding for project-scoped needs, and only use a ClusterRoleBinding if cluster-wide access is absolutely required. To close, ask: does this identity need actions across all namespaces, or only in a single project? Choose scope accordingly.

keyIdea.title: RBAC claim
keyIdea.text: Grant permissions with the narrowest scope that accomplishes the task: prefer Role + RoleBinding over cluster-scoped alternatives when possible.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › RBAC Fundamentals
RBAC primitives
  • Role: namespace-scoped permission set.
  • ClusterRole: cluster-scoped permission set.
  • RoleBinding: grants a Role or ClusterRole to a subject within a namespace.
  • ClusterRoleBinding: grants a ClusterRole cluster-wide.
Command example
oc policy add-role-to-user edit jane.doe -n my-dev-project
oc policy remove-role-from-user edit jane.doe -n my-dev-project
oc policy add-role-to-group admin dev-team -n my-dev-project
These policy commands create or remove RoleBindings for the given subject.
Misconceptions and guidance
  • Misconception: ClusterRoleBindings are just easier. Guidance: avoid cluster-wide bindings unless necessary.
  • Misconception: default roles are always sufficient. Guidance: review predefined roles and create custom Roles for specific needs.

screens.title: Role vs ClusterRole and Binding Types
screens.subtitle: Which to use and the security implications of scope

narration.text: Choosing between Role and ClusterRole, and between RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding, is an exercise in scoping permissions appropriately. A Role defines permissions inside one project: create it when a team only needs rights within a single namespace. A ClusterRole spans the cluster and is appropriate for cluster-level operators or tools that require access across many namespaces. The corresponding binding objects attach those permissions to users, groups, or service accounts. For instance, if you need the frontend-team to deploy into frontend-dev only, bind the edit ClusterRole using a RoleBinding within frontend-dev; that grants the team required actions in that project without giving them the ability to manage roles. The critical mistake is using ClusterRoleBinding because it is tempting and quick; it can elevate privileges cluster-wide. A useful mental model is to ask: does the identity need access across projects? If not, prefer a RoleBinding. Practical example: to let a service account read pods in its namespace, create a Role with get/list on pods and a RoleBinding to that service account. To check for over-permissioning, audit RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings regularly and look for unexpected subjects or bindings to high-privilege ClusterRoles like cluster-admin. The takeaway: scope first, widen only when justified.

keyIdea.title: Scope rule
keyIdea.text: Always prefer namespace-scoped Role + RoleBinding for project needs; reserve ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding for cluster-wide requirements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Role vs ClusterRole
Namespace-scoped (Role + RoleBinding)
Use when permissions are needed only inside a single project. Safer and easier to audit per team.
Example: a Role that grants pods get/list and a RoleBinding for the app service account.
Cluster-scoped (ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding)
Use only for cluster-level admins, operators, or cross-namespace tools that must operate everywhere.
Caution: ClusterRoleBindings can grant broad privileges if misapplied.
Audit guidance
  • List bindings and review subjects: oc get rolebindings -n <project> and oc get clusterrolebindings.
  • Look for bindings to cluster-admin or unexpected groups/users.

screens.title: Built-in ClusterRoles: admin, edit, view, cluster-admin
screens.subtitle: What each role gives you and when to use them

narration.text: OpenShift ships several default ClusterRoles that are convenient starting points. The admin role gives full control over a project, including role management within that project. The edit role grants read/write access to most resources but intentionally excludes role management and quota changes; it’s the right fit when a team needs to deploy and modify applications but not change permissions. The view role is read-only and suits auditors or dashboards. Finally, cluster-admin is the super-user role with unrestricted cluster privileges and should be reserved for trusted operators. A concrete example in scope: grant the frontend-team the edit ClusterRole via a RoleBinding in frontend-dev to allow deployments without letting them escalate privileges. A common mistake is granting admin or cluster-admin by habit; this can enable privilege escalation. Always ask what actions the subject must perform and match that to the narrowest built-in role, or create a custom Role when built-ins are too broad or too narrow. When in doubt, test by logging in as the subject and attempting a forbidden action so you can validate the role’s boundaries. This approach both protects the cluster and documents the minimal permissions required.

keyIdea.title: Role guidance
keyIdea.text: Prefer edit for project-level deployers, view for observers, admin only for project managers, and reserve cluster-admin for operators.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Built-in ClusterRoles
admin
Full control in a project, including role management. Use for project owners who manage members and quotas.
edit
Read/write for most resources but cannot manage roles. Ideal for developers and CI pipelines.
view
Read-only access for dashboards, auditors, or external review tools.
cluster-admin
Super-user access across the cluster. Only assign to trusted administrators and automation that truly needs cluster-wide privileges.

screens.title: Service Accounts: Identity for Applications
screens.subtitle: Create a service account, Role and RoleBinding, and apply with oc

narration.text: Service accounts are identities used by processes running inside pods to call the Kubernetes A P I. By default a pod gets a default service account in its namespace, but you should create named service accounts with narrowly scoped roles for applications. The process is straightforward: create the service account, define a Role that grants the exact verbs on the required resources, and bind that Role to the service account using a RoleBinding. For example, you might create a Role that allows get, list, and watch on deployments and services, then bind it to app-reader-sa so your application can discover resources but cannot change roles. Apply the Role and RoleBinding with oc apply and set the pod’s serviceAccountName in the Deployment to the named account. A common misconception is using the default service account for production workloads; that approach risks broad implicit permissions. After applying bindings, verify by exec-ing into a pod and running A P I calls expected to succeed and expected to fail. This validation confirms the principle of least privilege and helps you detect accidental over-permissioning. Service Accounts: Identity for Applications means create named service accounts, assign narrow roles, and bind them via rolebindings; never rely on the default account for production.. In practical terms, create a service account, role and rolebinding, and apply with oc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Service account pattern
keyIdea.text: Create named service accounts, assign narrow Roles, and bind them via RoleBindings; never rely on the default account for production.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Service Accounts
YAML example
# my-app-sa-role.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: my-dev-project
rules:
- apiGroups: [""] # "" indicates the core API group
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "watch", "list"]
---
# my-app-sa-rolebinding.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: pod-reader-binding
  namespace: my-dev-project
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: my-app-serviceaccount
  namespace: my-dev-project
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
Apply with: oc apply -f my-app-sa-role.yaml -n my-dev-project
Steps
  1. Create serviceaccount: oc create serviceaccount app-reader-sa -n my-dev-project
  2. Apply Role and RoleBinding manifests with oc apply.
  3. Set serviceAccountName in Deployment manifest and redeploy.
Check

Verify the service account cannot perform escalated actions such as changing roles or listing nodes.

screens.title: Principle of Least Privilege and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: How to avoid over-privileging and audit your bindings

narration.text: The principle of least privilege means granting only the permissions necessary for a user or service account to perform its job. In OpenShift this translates to: create narrow Roles, bind them in the smallest scope needed, and avoid granting admin or cluster-admin unless justified. A common error is granting admin or cluster-admin for convenience when edit or a custom Role would suffice. Another mistake is using ClusterRoleBinding where a RoleBinding would meet requirements, thereby escalating access cluster-wide. Regular audits close the loop: list rolebindings with oc get rolebindings -n <project> and clusterrolebindings to inspect who has access. When auditing, look for unexpected subjects, orphaned service accounts, and bindings to high-privilege ClusterRoles. Use external identity providers when possible so user lifecycle is managed by a centralized system, reducing stale accounts. Also be cautious with self-provisioner: it allows users to create projects and may need to be restricted in controlled environments. The behavioral guidance is to design for revocation: ensure you can quickly remove permissions when a developer leaves or automation changes. This reduces risk and keeps access aligned with current responsibilities.

keyIdea.title: Security principle
keyIdea.text: Grant minimal permissions, audit bindings regularly, and prefer external identity providers for enterprise environments.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Least Privilege & Audits
Practical checklist
  • Prefer Role + RoleBinding scoped to a project whenever possible.
  • Use edit for deployers, view for observers, and custom Roles for narrow needs.
  • Audit: oc get rolebindings -n <project> and oc get clusterrolebindings.
Common mistakes
  • Granting cluster-admin to automation that only needs namespace access.
  • Using default service accounts for production workloads.
  • Allowing self-provisioner broadly without governance.
Warning

ClusterRoleBindings are powerful. Review them frequently and restrict who can create them.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Create Project, Assign Roles, Configure a Service Account
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step terminal demo you will perform in the lab

narration.text: This lab walkthrough ties the chapter together into a repeatable set of administrator actions. First, log in as a cluster administrator. Then create a project using oc new-project my-app-project --display-name="My Application Development". Confirm you are assigned admin in the project. Next, create a test user and group or use an external identity provider if available. Example steps include creating an htpasswd user or using oc adm create-user and oc adm create-group, then adding the user to the group. Grant the devuser the edit role in the project with oc policy add-role-to-user edit devuser -n my-app-project, and bind the group with oc policy add-role-to-group admin dev-team -n my-app-project if appropriate. Verify as the developer: log in and confirm oc get pods -n my-app-project works but oc get nodes is forbidden. Switch back to admin, create a service account with oc create serviceaccount app-reader-sa -n my-app-project, apply a Role manifest to grant specific read permissions, then bind it to the service account. Finally, deploy or update a pod to use serviceAccountName: app-reader-sa and validate the pod’s permissions. This sequence builds confidence in scoping and verification.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Create a project, assign a user/group the edit role, create a service account with a custom Role, and verify permissions from the subject’s perspective.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Lab Walkthrough
Terminal sequence
# As cluster admin
oc login -u system:admin
oc new-project my-app-project --display-name="My Application Development"

# Create test user and group (if using HTPasswd or oc adm)
oc adm create-user devuser --full-name="Developer User"
oc adm create-group dev-team
oc adm add-user-to-group dev-team devuser

# Grant edit role
oc policy add-role-to-user edit devuser -n my-app-project
# Or bind group to admin if owners need role management
oc policy add-role-to-group admin dev-team -n my-app-project
After granting roles, test by logging in as devuser and confirming expected access.
Service account steps
oc create serviceaccount app-reader-sa -n my-app-project
# apply Role and RoleBinding YAML from earlier
oc apply -f app-reader-role.yaml -n my-app-project
oc apply -f app-reader-rolebinding.yaml -n my-app-project
Update your Deployment to use serviceAccountName: app-reader-sa and redeploy to test behavior.
Validation

As the developer, oc get nodes should be forbidden; oc get pods -n my-app-project should succeed. Test both success and failure cases.

screens.title: Assessment Ideas and Reflection
screens.subtitle: Questions and scenarios to test understanding

narration.text: To assess comprehension, use scenario-based questions that force a decision about scope and privileges. For example, present a team that needs full control over application resources but must not change roles: ask which built-in ClusterRole to bind and whether to use a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding. The correct choice is to bind the edit ClusterRole within the project using a RoleBinding. Another assessment asks why a pod cannot list secrets in another project even though its service account exists: this tests knowledge that RoleBindings are namespace-scoped and cross-project access must be explicitly granted. Practical assessment tasks include creating a project, adding a user to a group, granting the edit role, and demonstrating that the user cannot perform cluster-admin actions like listing nodes. For service accounts, test creating a Role and RoleBinding, deploying a pod with that service account, and verifying the pod can perform permitted A P I calls but not others. When grading, ensure learners justify their choices by explaining scope, verbs, and resources used. This shows applied understanding, not just rote command knowledge. Reflection

When you design access, name the actor, the actions required, and the smallest scope that satisfies the need. This method prevents accidental privilege escalation.

narration.text: These core concepts summarize the chapter and should guide your day-to-day decisions. First, a project is an OpenShift-enhanced namespace: it groups resources, holds annotations, and serves as a boundary for role bindings and quotas. Second, RBAC uses Roles and ClusterRoles to declare permissions and RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings to assign those permissions to users, groups, or service accounts. Understand the difference in scope and prefer the least-privilege option. Third, service accounts are the identities for workloads; create named service accounts with narrow Roles and bind them so applications have only the permissions they need. Keep these three ideas in mind as you design access and ownership for teams and automation. narration.text: These implementation reminders help you act safely when configuring projects and permissions. First, always verify scope: prefer RoleBindings in a project rather than ClusterRoleBindings when possible. Second, avoid using default service accounts for production; create named service accounts and attach narrowly-scoped Roles. Third, adopt auditing and external identity providers for enterprise environments so user lifecycle and access changes are centrally managed. Keep these reminders in mind when you write manifests and apply oc commands; they reduce risk and make your access model easier to audit and maintain. Prefer RoleBinding
Favor project-scoped bindings unless cluster scope is required.
Named service accounts
Give apps explicit identities and scoped permissions.
Centralize identity
Use LDAP or OpenID Connect for user lifecycle and policy enforcement.

Design with scope and revocation in mind: minimal permissions that you can remove quickly are safer for production clusters.
